strengths: Addresses an important problem: preference optimization for masked discrete diffusion models using an implementable stepwise loss that does not require differentiating through the full sampling trajectory.
Experiments span three domains, including an 8B language model. DNA results improve several metrics over DRAKES, and language results improve across GSM8K, IFEval, and AlpacaEval.

Biological experiments use separate training and evaluation reward predictors and report results across three seeds. Hyperparameter details and ablations on sample count, regularization, and iterative labeling provide useful empirical context.
weaknesses: The central equivalence theorem has a fundamental mathematical error. In Eqs. 10 and 15, the exponential tilt uses the expected reward r̂_t(x_t,c), which is constant with respect to x_0. Normalization therefore cancels this factor, yielding p*=p_ref rather than the optimizer of Eq. 9 for a nonconstant reward. The optimizer of Eq. 9 must instead involve r(x_0,c). This is substantive: the proof explicitly relies on pulling the constant reward outside the sum in Eqs. 17–19.

The trajectory proof also incorrectly drops the product of state-dependent normalizers between Eqs. 22 and 23. These cannot generally be absorbed into a trajectory-independent partition function. Correcting the reward argument alone does not repair the claimed equivalence; additive trajectory rewards do not establish that independently optimized clean-sequence conditionals induce the globally optimal trajectory distribution.

The distribution-matching derivation does not justify the implemented loss. Eq. 11 again defines its reward distribution using an x_0-independent expected reward, whereas Appendix A.3 silently replaces this with sample-specific rewards. Furthermore, conditional importance sampling requires candidates from p_ref(x_0|x_t,c) at a shared x_t, but the implementation compares candidates with separately corrupted x_t values. Training also uses original datasets and iteratively generated samples without establishing the required reference sampling distribution or providing a correction. Proposition 4.3 therefore does not establish consistency for the actual training procedure.

The empirical comparisons do not isolate the proposed contribution sufficiently. Language experiments compare only against the unchanged reference model, omitting matched supervised finetuning and alternative diffusion preference objectives. Biological baseline numbers are imported from prior work without matched compute and tuning budgets. There is no direct ablation of the proposed timestep weighting and no measured training-time or memory comparison supporting the efficiency claims.

Claims of consistent superiority and robustness exceed the evidence. In Table 2, SDPO increases predicted stability but reduces joint success from 78.6% to 75.5% and structural-threshold success from 91.8% to 88.9% relative to DRAKES. Appendix C.2 reports a different operating point that matches joint success, but its selection protocol is unclear. Biological gains remain predictor-based, and language improvements lack uncertainty estimates. These promising empirical results do not compensate for the invalid theoretical foundation presented as a principal contribution.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: preference optimization for masked discrete diffusion models, with an implementable objective supporting numerical rewards and preference pairs.
Experiments span three domains. Table 1 reports improvements across all five DNA evaluation metrics, and language results improve on all three benchmarks.
The biological experiments use separate training and evaluation reward predictors and report results across three seeds. Hyperparameter details and ablations provide useful implementation context.
weaknesses: The central optimality claim is mathematically incorrect as written. In Eq. 10, the reward hat-r_t(x_t,c) is independent of x_0, so its exponential cancels against the conditional normalizer, yielding p*=p_ref. This generally cannot optimize Eq. 9 for nonconstant rewards. The correct exponential tilt for Eq. 9 depends on r(x_0,c). This error recurs throughout the proofs and distribution-matching formulation.

Theorem 4.1 has additional substantive proof failures. Appendix A.1 drops the product of state-dependent partition functions between Eqs. 22 and 23; these cannot generally be absorbed into one trajectory-independent normalizer. Replacing the reward in Eq. 15 with r(x_0,c) would also invalidate the step pulling its exponential outside the sum in Eq. 18. Consequently, the claimed equivalence between stepwise optimization and trajectory optimization is not established by a simple notation correction.

The practical loss is not justified by the stated consistency argument. Eq. 11 defines conditional distribution matching at fixed x_t, whereas Eqs. 12–13 normalize across samples with different x_t values. Appendix A.3 also substitutes r(x_0,c) for hat-r_t(x_t,c) without justification. Forward-corrupting offline samples does not generally produce samples from the learned reverse conditional required by the importance-sampling derivation. Proposition 4.3 therefore does not establish consistency of the implemented objective.

The evaluation does not sufficiently isolate the proposed contribution. Language experiments compare only against the unmodified checkpoint, without matched supervised fine-tuning or alternative preference objectives. Biological baselines are imported from prior work, and there is no matched comparison against simpler reward-weighted training. The reported gains consequently do not establish the necessity of the proposed decomposition.

Claims of consistently superior performance and resistance to reward overoptimization exceed the evidence. In Table 2, protein success rate falls from DRAKES' 78.6% to 75.5%, and structural fidelity worsens despite higher predicted reward. Appendix C.2 provides a more balanced operating point that matches success rate, but does not establish uniform superiority. Separate learned evaluators offer useful corroboration, not proof of biological validity or absence of reward exploitation.

Efficiency and language-model improvements need stronger supporting evidence. The paper reports reduced labeling requirements but no matched wall-clock, total-compute, or memory comparison. Language results lack repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. These empirical limitations matter especially because the central theoretical guarantees fail.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: preference optimization for masked discrete diffusion models using tractable denoiser likelihoods and rewards on clean sequences.
Experiments span three domains and include an 8B language model. The reported language results improve across GSM8K, IFEval, and AlpacaEval, providing encouraging evidence of practical utility.

The biological sequence experiments include separately trained evaluation predictors, multiple quality metrics, and results across three seeds. Ablations investigate sample count, regularization, and iterative labeling, and the appendix provides useful training details.
weaknesses: The central optimality guarantee is mathematically incorrect as written. The optimizer of Eq. 9 should be proportional to pref(x0|xt,c) exp(r(x0,c)/βt). Instead, Eq. 10 uses the expected reward r̂t(xt,c), which is constant with respect to x0 at fixed xt,c and therefore cancels under normalization, leaving exactly the reference distribution. This error recurs in Appendix A.1 and the distribution-matching formulation, so it undermines the main theoretical contribution rather than constituting an isolated typographical mistake.

Theorem 4.1 has an additional substantive proof error: the transition from Eq. 22 to Eq. 23 drops the product of conditional partition functions. These generally depend on the intermediate states and cannot be discarded or absorbed into a context-only normalizer. Replacing the expected reward with r(x0,c) would also invalidate its extraction from the sum in Eqs. 17–18. Consequently, the claimed equivalence between independent stepwise optimization and global trajectory optimization is not established.

The practical estimator does not follow from the stated conditional KL objective. Estimating its normalizers requires multiple completions conditioned on the same xt,c, whereas Eqs. 12–13 compare samples with different corrupted states xt^(i). Section 4.4 further substitutes forward-corrupted clean samples for reverse-process samples without establishing distributional equivalence. The appendix also switches from exp(r̂t) to exp(r) without justification. Proposition 4.3 therefore does not establish consistency for the implemented training procedure.

The empirical comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. Language experiments compare only against the unaligned reference model, lacking matched preference-finetuning baselines. Biological baseline numbers are inherited from prior work, while SDPO uses multiple training stages and changing hyperparameters. There are no direct runtime or memory comparisons supporting the efficiency claims, and language results lack uncertainty estimates.

Claims of consistent superiority and resistance to reward overoptimization exceed the evidence. In Table 2, SDPO improves predicted stability but reduces joint success from 78.6% to 75.5% and worsens structural consistency relative to DRAKES. Appendix Table 9 provides a better-balanced configuration that matches the baseline success rate, but does not establish uniform superiority. Predictor-based biological evaluations also cannot establish experimentally validated activity or stability.

strengths: Addresses a timely problem: preference alignment of discrete diffusion models without differentiating through full sampling trajectories or requiring differentiable rewards.

Demonstrates applicability across three domains, including an 8B language model. Reported language results improve GSM8K from 78.6 to 81.2, IFEval from 52.9 to 55.1, and AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate from 10.6 to 14.2.

The biological benchmarks include multiple quality and diversity metrics, separate training and evaluation reward predictors, and results over three seeds. These provide more informative evidence than optimization-reward scores alone.
Includes useful ablations on regularization, sample-group size, dataset size, and iterative labeling, along with training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The implemented loss is not a consistent estimator of the conditional distribution-matching objective that motivates it. Equation 10 normalizes across samples with different corrupted inputs, whereas Equation 9 requires a separate conditional partition function for each input. Increasing N does not generally remove this mismatch. The paper acknowledges bias but provides neither a bound nor evidence that the surrogate preserves the claimed optimum, leaving the central theoretical guarantee disconnected from the algorithm.

Theorem 4.1 establishes optimality for a specially constructed trajectory reward derived from the tilted transition kernels. It does not establish equivalence to optimizing the original terminal reward, or an arbitrary prescribed additive trajectory reward. This is a substantially narrower result than the broad trajectory-alignment framing suggests.

Proposition 4.2 assumes that the parameterized model can exactly match the reward-tilted distribution. This realizability assumption is unstated and particularly problematic for factorized masked-token predictions: arbitrary sequence-level rewards can introduce dependencies that the single-pass prediction distribution cannot represent. Compatibility of the stepwise optima under shared parameters is also not established.

The sampling assumptions behind the importance-sampling derivation do not match the experiments. Training uses original datasets and externally generated language preferences rather than samples from the reference model. Iterative training can also use samples from an updated model while retaining the original reference. No proposal correction or analysis establishes that the stated objective remains valid under these discrepancies.

Empirical superiority is overstated. In Table 2, higher predicted stability accompanies lower joint success than DRAKES (75.5% versus 78.6%) and a lower structural-consistency pass rate (88.9% versus 91.8%). Appendix C.3 provides a more balanced configuration, but it matches rather than exceeds the baseline's success rate. The evidence supports a tradeoff, not consistent dominance.

The evaluation does not sufficiently isolate the contribution of the objective. Baselines lack clearly documented matched data, iterative-labeling, tuning, and compute budgets; language experiments omit uncertainty estimates and simple supervised or reward-weighted fine-tuning controls. There is also no ablation of the timestep weighting or direct assessment of the conditional-normalization approximation. Efficiency claims rely primarily on complexity analysis and labeling counts rather than measured end-to-end runtime and memory.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: preference optimization for discrete diffusion models without differentiating through complete sampling trajectories. The proposed training loss is simple and accommodates both scalar rewards and pairwise preferences.

Evaluation spans three substantially different domains, including an 8B language model. Reported improvements include GSM8K accuracy from 78.6 to 81.2 and AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate from 10.6 to 14.2.

The biological experiments include multiple quality and diversity metrics, separately trained evaluation reward models, and three-seed results. Appendices provide training hyperparameters and additional ablations.
weaknesses: The implemented loss is not established as an estimator of the theoretical conditional objective. Equation 9 requires a partition function conditional on a particular noisy input x_t, whereas Equation 10 normalizes across samples with different noisy inputs. Increasing N therefore does not generally recover the required conditional normalizer. The paper acknowledges this approximation but provides neither a consistency argument nor an experiment isolating its consequences, leaving the central theoretical guarantee disconnected from the actual algorithm.

Additional assumptions behind the derivation are insufficiently justified. Appendix A.3 replaces conditional reward normalization with a joint reward-tilted distribution without specifying the required marginal distribution over x_t. Section 4.4 further replaces reference-model trajectory samples with forward-corrupted clean samples, which need not have the same joint distribution. The experimental datasets and iteratively generated samples also do not generally follow the fixed reference proposal assumed in the derivation.

Theorem 4.1 establishes optimality for a specially constructed trajectory reward derived from the induced transition likelihood ratios. It does not establish equivalence to optimizing the original terminal reward r(x_0,c), or an independently specified additive trajectory reward. Furthermore, Proposition 4.2 assumes exact distribution matching is attainable; arbitrary sequence-level reward tilting need not be representable by the token-factorized denoiser. These limitations substantially narrow the advertised equivalence.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the proposed method's contribution. Headline biological results use iterative generation and relabeling, alongside substantial changes in N, regularization, learning rate, and sometimes the reference checkpoint. The baseline comparisons do not establish matched data, tuning, and compute budgets. Ablations of the weighting schedule and comparisons against simple reward-weighted fine-tuning would help distinguish the benefit of the proposed decomposition from established distribution-matching objectives.

Claims of consistent superiority overstate the results. In Table 2, protein folding success falls from DRAKES's 78.6% to 75.5%, and the proportion satisfying the structural threshold falls from 91.8% to 88.9%, despite improved predicted stability. Appendix Table 10 provides a better-balanced run matching the baseline success rate, but does not specify its selection protocol or uncertainty. Predictor-based evaluations support computational improvements, not definitive biological effectiveness or robustness against reward exploitation.

Language-model evidence and efficiency validation remain limited. Table 3 compares only the reference model and D2-DPO, without repeated-run uncertainty or sufficient baseline training details. The claimed computational benefits are supported by asymptotic analysis and labeling counts rather than measured training time, peak memory, or total cost including iterative generation. Overall, the promising empirical results do not compensate for the unresolved connection between the theory and implemented objective.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: efficient preference optimization for discrete diffusion models, with a practical objective supporting scalar rewards and pairwise preferences.

The evaluation spans three domains and includes relevant discrete-diffusion alignment baselines. The biological experiments report three-seed results and use separate training and evaluation reward models.

Reported improvements are promising: DNA predicted activity rises from 5.61 to 6.30 over DRAKES, alongside improvements in several complementary metrics. LLaDA improves on GSM8K, IFEval, and AlpacaEval relative to both the reference model and D2-DPO.
Ablations investigate regularization strength, sample count, iterative labeling, and dataset size, and the appendix provides useful training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The implemented loss is not established as an optimizer of the theoretical objective. Equation 10 normalizes scores across samples with different corrupted states, whereas Equation 9 requires a separate conditional partition function for each fixed state. Increasing N does not generally eliminate this mismatch. The paper acknowledges the approximation but provides neither a consistency argument nor an experiment quantifying its consequences, leaving the central optimality guarantee disconnected from the actual algorithm.

Theorem 4.1 establishes optimality for a specially constructed trajectory reward defined through the induced transition ratios. It does not establish equivalence to optimizing the original terminal reward, or an independently specified additive trajectory reward. This is a narrower result than the paper's broad trajectory-alignment framing suggests.

Proposition 4.2 assumes that the model can exactly represent the reward-tilted conditional distribution and attain zero KL. Standard parallel masked-token predictors factorize their output distributions, while arbitrary sequence-level rewards generally introduce dependencies. The paper does not state the necessary realizability assumptions or explain how simultaneous optimization with shared parameters affects its guarantees.

The importance-sampling derivation assumes samples from the reference joint distribution. The actual experiments instead use original training data, an external language preference dataset, and samples from updated models; forward corruption also need not reproduce the learned reverse-process joint. These distribution mismatches are not corrected or adequately analyzed.

The empirical results do not establish consistent superiority across meaningful outcomes. In Table 2, SDPO improves predicted stability but reduces protein success rate from 78.6% to 75.5% and structural validity from 91.8% to 88.9%. Appendix C.3 provides a configuration matching the baseline success rate, which is useful, but does not support an unqualified superiority claim. Biological validation remains computational.

Comparative attribution and efficiency evidence are incomplete. The strongest biological results use iterative data collection, but competing offline methods are not evaluated under a clearly matched iterative protocol and tuning budget. No measured training-time or peak-memory comparison substantiates the efficiency claims. Language results lack uncertainty estimates, and the pairwise objective's close relationship to existing diffusion DPO leaves the distinct contribution insufficiently isolated.
